claims.text: The starting Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is an as-cast solid-solution alloy.
FeNiCrMn is produced by removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Removing Co reduces deformation-twinning activity in FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
Removing Co promotes dislocation glide in FeNiCrMn relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
The shift from twinning toward dislocation glide enables a favorable strength–ductility balance over varied temperatures and strain rates.
In situ neutron diffraction coupled with TEM can be used to characterize evolving deformation structures during loading.
The proposed comparison spans quasi-static rates through approximately 10^3 s^-1 and room temperature through approximately 900°C.
The FeNiCrMn alloy can be maintained as a single-phase solid solution throughout the proposed temperature and strain-rate regime.
The relevant structural mediator is the relative density and evolution kinetics of deformation twins and mobile dislocation structures.
Eliminating Co alters the stacking-fault energy of FeNiCrMn.
Eliminating Co alters local lattice distortion in FeNiCrMn.
The proposed changes in stacking-fault energy and local lattice distortion suppress mechanical twinning and favor dislocation glide.
The twinning-to-glide shift changes strain hardening and thereby maintains the strength–ductility balance during dynamic loading.
At high strain rates and elevated temperatures, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have a lower twin density than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi tested under identical conditions.
At high strain rates and elevated temperatures, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have higher dislocation mobility than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, Co-free FeNiCrMn will show a modest reduction in strain-hardening rate while preserving favorable strength and ductility.
The hypothesis applies only while precipitation or phase decomposition is absent, and phase instability may cause deviations.
Failure to observe lower twin density or higher dislocation mobility together with a distinguishable strain-hardening response would falsify the hypothesis.
